title: Automatic updates — the questions before anything is drawn

steps.path: Settings → Help & feedback, and the version chip's update popup
steps.headline: Should there be a switch to turn automatic updates off, and where?
steps.today: Nothing installs unless you open the version chip's popup and press Update now. The only update setting is "Get beta builds", which sits in Settings → Help & feedback and under the release notes in that popup.
steps.problem: Once updates download and install by themselves, someone who wants to stay on a version (a class demo, a flaky connection, a known-good setup) has no way to say no.
steps.proposal: A switch, "Install updates automatically", on unless you turn it off. Off brings back today's behaviour: you are told about the update and press the button yourself.

options.label: Beside Get beta builds
options.summary: In Settings → Help & feedback and in the update popup, right next to the beta switch.
pros: Sits with the only other update setting, so both are found together.
Reachable from the moment you see an update, without hunting through settings.
cons: Two more rows on a popup that is mostly release notes.

options.label: Settings only
pros: The update popup stays as short as it is today.
cons: Someone surprised by an update has to know to look in Settings.

options.label: No switch
pros: One less setting; everyone stays current.
cons: No way to hold back an update, even for a good reason.

steps.path: The version label at the bottom right of the window
steps.headline: What should the version chip look like once an update is downloaded and waiting?
steps.today: When a new version exists the chip turns yellow, pulses gently, and reads "v1.3.2 — Update available" until you install it, which can be days.
steps.problem: With updates downloading by themselves, "Update available" is no longer true — it is already here and will install the next time you quit. A pulsing chip for something that will happen on its own is nagging.
steps.proposal: Change the words to say it is ready, and decide whether it keeps calling for attention.

options.label: Calm "Update ready"
options.summary: A plain chip reading "v1.4.0 ready — restart to update", with the yellow tint but no pulse.
pros: Tells you it is there without asking you to act.
Nothing moves in the corner of your eye while you work.
cons: Easier to overlook if you want the update right away.

options.label: Pulse as today
pros: Hard to miss.
cons: Keeps pulsing for something that needs nothing from you.

options.label: No change until it installs
options.summary: The chip shows the version you have; the next launch shows the new one.
pros: Completely invisible.
cons: No way to know a restart would bring the fix you are waiting for.

steps.path: Version chip → popup → Restart to update
steps.headline: If a chat is still working when you press Restart to update, should the app ask first?
steps.today: Update now closes the app straight away; a reply in the middle of being written stops there.
steps.problem: Restart to update is meant to be a one-click convenience, but a reply cut off halfway, or a long task stopped, costs real work.
steps.proposal: Check for chats that are still working before restarting.

options.label: Ask only if busy
options.summary: "2 chats are still working. Restart anyway?" with Restart and Wait. Restarts at once when nothing is working.
pros: One click when idle, a safety net when not.
Matches how quitting an app with unsaved work usually behaves.
cons: One more click on the occasions a chat is busy.

options.label: Wait, then restart
options.summary: The button becomes "Restarting when chats finish…" and restarts on its own once nothing is working.
pros: Never interrupts work, never asks.
cons: The app restarts at a moment you did not pick, possibly while you are reading.

options.label: Just restart
pros: Simplest.
cons: Loses whatever the busy chats were in the middle of.

steps.path: Linux installs from a .deb, .rpm or .pacman package (including yours)
steps.headline: On Linux package installs, which need your password, when should the update ask for it?
steps.today: Pressing Update now on a package install downloads the update, then shows the system's password box; after that it installs and restarts.
steps.problem: "Install when you quit" cannot work here without a password box popping up just as you close the app. Windows, Mac and the single-file Linux version need no password.
steps.proposal: Pick when the password box appears on these installs.

options.label: Only on Restart to update
options.summary: It still downloads by itself; the chip says it is ready; the password box appears only when you press Restart to update.
pros: A password box never appears without you asking for it.
Same button and chip as every other computer.
cons: Quitting does not install it, so these installs stay behind until you press the button.

options.label: Ask while quitting
pros: Installs as close to automatically as Linux allows.
cons: A password box after you close the app is surprising, and easy to dismiss by accident.

steps.path: The YouCoded app in the Mac's Applications folder
steps.headline: If a Mac will not let YouCoded replace itself, is falling back to today's drag-to-Applications step acceptable?
steps.today: Mac updates open a disk image and you drag the new app into Applications yourself.
steps.problem: The new automatic swap works when the person who installed YouCoded is the one using it (the usual case). On a Mac account that is not an administrator, the swap is refused.
steps.proposal: Yes: in that case the popup says it could not install automatically and opens the disk image as today. No: we look for another way first (for example asking for an administrator password), which is more work and new behaviour to design.

steps.intro: For when a release turns out to be broken. These two decide how it is pulled and what people see.

steps.path: Behind the scenes, on the release itself
steps.headline: How should a broken release be pulled?
steps.today: Every release carries a signed list of its installers. Without that list, YouCoded refuses to install the release, but it still says an update is available.
steps.problem: Once updates install themselves, a broken release reaches everyone within hours. Pulling it must be one step, and must stop computers that downloaded it but have not installed it yet.
steps.proposal: Two ways to build the brake. Either way you ask me ("pull 1.4.0") and I do it; nothing for you to run.

options.label: Pull the release's signed list
options.summary: I remove the signed list and mark the release as not the latest, which also takes it off the website. Updated apps stop offering it; apps that already downloaded it check again before installing and drop it.
pros: Uses what already exists; nothing new on our server.
Even today's 1.3.2 installs already refuse a release without the list.
cons: Takes effect when each app next checks: up to about 30 minutes.

options.label: A switch on our server
options.summary: A new on/off setting on the marketplace server that the app reads before offering or installing anything.
pros: Could later grow into gradual rollout (sending a release to a few people first).
cons: New server work to build and keep running.
Only apps from this release onward would obey it.

steps.path: The announcement chip in the status bar
steps.headline: Should people who already installed a pulled release see a message?
steps.today: There is an announcement chip (orange star) we can turn on for everyone with one line in a file; it is how notices reach people today.
steps.problem: Pulling a release stops new installs, but whoever already has it keeps it until the fix arrives, without knowing anything is wrong.
steps.proposal: Choose whether pulling also tells them.

options.label: Use the announcement chip
options.summary: Nothing automatic. When a problem is worth telling people about, I post a notice through the existing announcement chip.
pros: No new screens to build.
You decide case by case whether a notice helps or only worries people.
cons: Reaches everyone, including people who never installed the broken release.

options.label: Automatic notice
options.summary: Apps on a pulled release show "This version has a known problem — a fix is on the way" in the version chip.
pros: Only the people affected see it.
cons: A new message to design and build.
It can sound more alarming than the problem deserves.

options.label: Say nothing
pros: Simplest; the fix simply arrives as an update.
cons: People hitting the problem do not know help is coming.
